A counterexample to a conjecture of Duncan on versal actions

Federico Scavia Address: CNRS
Institut Galilée
Université Sorbonne Paris Nord
99 avenue Jean-Baptiste Clément, 93430
Villetaneuse, France Email address: scavia@math.univ-paris13.fr
Date: July 27, 2026
Abstract.

We disprove a conjecture of Duncan asserting that versality of a faithful finite group action can be detected on Sylow subgroups. Our counterexample is an action of (C7⋊C3)×C2(C_{7}\rtimes C_{3})\times C_{2} on a degree-22 Del Pezzo surface.

Key words and phrases:
Versal action, essential dimension, Del Pezzo surface, Sylow subgroup, twisting, unirationality
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14L30; Secondary 14E08, 14G05, 20D20

1. Introduction

Let kk be a field, and let GG be a finite group. By definition, a kk-variety is a separated kk-scheme of finite type, and a GG-variety is a kk-variety together with a left GG-action over kk. Among GG-varieties, versal GG-varieties (see §2 for the definition) play a special role. For example, the essential dimension edk⁡(G)\operatorname{ed}_{k}(G) of GG over kk may be defined as the smallest dimension of a versal faithful GG-variety over kk. The following conjecture was formulated by Duncan [Dun13].

Conjecture 1.1 (Duncan).

Let kk be a field, and let GG be a finite group acting faithfully on a kk-variety XX. For every prime pp, let GpG_{p} be a Sylow pp-subgroup of GG. Then XX is GG-versal if and only if XX is GpG_{p}-versal for every prime pp.

Duncan formulated Conjecture 1.1 while classifying finite groups of essential dimension 22. For a smooth complete toric variety, he used Cox rings and universal torsors to prove that versality is detected on Sylow subgroups [Dun13, Corollary 3.6]. Since versality is a birational invariant, this led him to Conjecture 1.1.

Duncan and Reichstein placed Conjecture 1.1 in a broader framework relating versality to rational points on twisted varieties [DR15]. They characterized weak versality, versality, very versality, and pp-versality in terms of rational points on all twists of XX. Their results illustrate the subtlety of Conjecture 1.1: indeed, the weaker hypothesis of pp-versality for every prime pp does not imply versality in general, even for the trivial group over a non-algebraically closed field kk. The reason is that a kk-variety with a zero-cycle of degree one need not have a Zariski-dense set of kk-points; it need not even have a kk-point.

Several results in [DR15] may be viewed as special cases or close analogues of Conjecture 1.1. For projective space, the corresponding twists are Severi–Brauer varieties, and all notions of versality are equivalent to the existence of a lift of the projective action to a linear representation; see [DR15, Proposition 9.1]. For quadrics, Springer’s theorem yields a positive criterion involving a Sylow 22-subgroup [DR15, Theorem 10.2]. For smooth cubic hypersurfaces, the analogous statement is related to the Cassels–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture; see [DR15, Theorem 10.5]. Conjecture 1.1 also enters the discussion of the Klein cubic threefold: Duncan and Reichstein showed that it would imply edℂ⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))≤3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{11}))\leq 3, thus completing the classification of finite simple groups of essential dimension 33; see [DR15, Example 10.7].

We show that Conjecture 1.1 is false already in dimension 22. In fact, we prove something stronger: there exists a non-versal GG-action on a rational surface SS whose restriction to every Sylow subgroup of GG is very versal (see §2 for the definition).

Theorem 1.2.

Let ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C} be a primitive seventh root of unity, and let

S={w2=x3y+y3z+z3x}⊂ℙ(1,1,1,2).S=\{w^{2}=x^{3}y+y^{3}z+z^{3}x\}\subset\mathbb{P}(1,1,1,2).

The surface SS is a Del Pezzo11 1 I write Del Pezzo, rather than del Pezzo, following contemporary official usage. In particular, documents produced during Pasquale Del Pezzo’s lifetime and preserved in his personal file at the Historical Archive of the Italian Senate record his name as “Del Pezzo Pasquale”; see Archivio storico del Senato della Repubblica, Del Pezzo Pasquale. I thank Matteo Tamiozzo for bringing this usage to my attention and for providing the link. surface of degree 22. Let

G≔⟨ρ,σ,τ:ρ7=σ3=τ2=[τ,ρ]=[τ,σ]=1,σρσ−1=ρ4⟩≃(C7⋊C3)×C2.G\coloneqq\langle\rho,\sigma,\tau:\rho^{7}=\sigma^{3}=\tau^{2}=[\tau,\rho]=[\tau,\sigma]=1,\sigma\rho\sigma^{-1}=\rho^{4}\rangle\simeq(C_{7}\rtimes C_{3})\times C_{2}.

The formulas

ρ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\rho[x:y:z:w] =[ζx:ζ4y:ζ2z:w],\displaystyle=[\zeta x:\zeta^{4}y:\zeta^{2}z:w],
σ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\sigma[x:y:z:w] =[y:z:x:w],\displaystyle=[y:z:x:w],
τ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\tau[x:y:z:w] =[x:y:z:−w]\displaystyle=[x:y:z:-w]

define a faithful GG-action on SS.

  1. (1)

    The restriction of the action to every Sylow subgroup of GG is very versal.

  2. (2)

    We have edℂ⁡(G)=3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)=3, and hence the action of GG on SS is not versal.

For each Sylow subgroup GpG_{p} of GG, we construct a nonconstant GpG_{p}-equivariant morphism ℙℂ1→S\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\to S. Using a theorem of Salgado–Testa–Várilly-Alvarado [STV14, Theorem 17], we show that every twist of SS by a GpG_{p}-torsor is unirational. The criterion of Duncan–Reichstein (Proposition 2.1) then implies that the GpG_{p}-action on SS is very versal for every prime pp. On the other hand, it is not difficult to see that edℂ⁡(G)=3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)=3; in particular, the GG-action on the surface SS is not versal.

The surface SS and the action of GG already appeared in [Dun16, Example 1.9]. Duncan observed that every abelian subgroup of GG has a fixed point on SS and that edℂ⁡(G)>2\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)>2. The novel part of Theorem 1.2 is that the restriction of the action to every Sylow subgroup of GG is very versal, and hence versal.

2. Preliminaries on versality

Let kk be a field, let HH be a finite discrete group, and let XX be an integral HH-variety. Following [DR15], we say that XX is

  1. (i)

    weakly versal if, for every infinite field extension K/kK/k and every HH-torsor TT over KK, there exists an HH-equivariant kk-morphism T→XT\to X;

  2. (ii)

    versal if every dense HH-invariant open subvariety of XX is weakly versal;

  3. (iii)

    very versal if there exist a finite-dimensional kk-linear HH-representation VV and a dominant HH-equivariant rational map V⇢XV\dashrightarrow X.

Very versality implies versality, and versality implies weak versality; see [DR15, Equation (1.1)].

Let K/kK/k be an infinite field extension and let T→Spec⁡KT\to\operatorname{Spec}K be a right HH-torsor. The pair (T,K)(T,K) is called an HH-twisting pair. If XX is an HH-variety, its twist is

XT=(T×kX)/H,{}^{T}\!X=(T\times_{k}X)/H,

where HH acts on T×kXT\times_{k}X on the right by

(t,x)⋅h=(t​h,h−1​x).(t,x)\cdot h=(th,h^{-1}x).

The variety XT{}^{T}\!X is a KK-form of XKX_{K}. Twisting by a fixed HH-twisting pair is functorial with respect to HH-equivariant morphisms and HH-equivariant rational maps.

Proposition 2.1 (Duncan–Reichstein).

Let kk be a field, let HH be a finite discrete group, and let XX be an integral quasi-projective HH-variety. Then:

  1. (i)

    XX is weakly versal if and only if XT​(K)≠∅{}^{T}\!X(K)\neq\varnothing for every HH-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K);

  2. (ii)

    XX is versal if and only if XT​(K){}^{T}\!X(K) is Zariski dense in XT{}^{T}\!X for every HH-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K);

  3. (iii)

    XX is very versal if and only if XT{}^{T}\!X is KK-unirational for every HH-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K).

Proof.

See [DR15, Theorem 1.1(a)–(c)]. ∎

The following criterion for very versality of group actions on degree-22 Del Pezzo surfaces, based on a theorem of Salgado–Testa–Várilly-Alvarado [STV14, Theorem 17], will be used in the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Lemma 2.2.

Let HH be a cyclic group, let XX be a degree-22 Del Pezzo surface over ℂ\mathbb{C} with an action of HH. Suppose that there is a nonconstant HH-equivariant morphism ν:ℙℂ1→X\nu:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\to X. Then XX is HH-very versal.

Proof.

Let hh be a generator of HH. Choose a lift of the image of hh in PGL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) to an element of GL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). Since ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraically closed, this lift has an eigenvector. The corresponding ℂ\mathbb{C}-point of ℙℂ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}} is fixed by hh, and hence by HH.

Let (T,K)(T,K) be an HH-twisting pair. Twisting ν\nu gives a morphism

νT:(ℙℂ1)T⟶XT.{}^{T}\!\nu:{}^{T}\!(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}})\longrightarrow{}^{T}\!X.

The HH-fixed point of ℙℂ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}} descends to a KK-point of (ℙℂ1)T{}^{T}\!(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}). Since (ℙℂ1)T{}^{T}\!(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}) is a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus zero over KK, it is isomorphic to ℙK1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{K}. The twist XT{}^{T}\!X is again a degree-22 Del Pezzo surface, and the morphism νT{}^{T}\!\nu is nonconstant, since it becomes isomorphic to ν\nu after extending scalars to a splitting field of TT. By a theorem of Salgado–Testa–Várilly-Alvarado [STV14, Theorem 17], a degree-22 Del Pezzo surface in characteristic zero admitting a nonconstant morphism from ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} is unirational. Thus XT{}^{T}\!X is KK-unirational for every HH-twisting pair, and Proposition 2.1(iii) shows that XX is HH-very versal. ∎

3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We now prove Theorem 1.2. Let x,y,zx,y,z be homogeneous coordinates on ℙℂ2\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}, and let x,y,z,wx,y,z,w be weighted homogeneous coordinates on ℙ⁡(1,1,1,2)\mathbb{P}(1,1,1,2). Set

f(x,y,z)≔x3y+y3z+z3x,B≔{f(x,y,z)=0}⊂ℙℂ2,f(x,y,z)\coloneqq x^{3}y+y^{3}z+z^{3}x,\qquad B\coloneqq\{f(x,y,z)=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}},

and let π:S→ℙℂ2\pi:S\to\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}} be the double cover ramified over BB:

S≔{w2=f(x,y,z)}⊂ℙ(1,1,1,2).S\coloneqq\{w^{2}=f(x,y,z)\}\subset\mathbb{P}(1,1,1,2).

The curve BB is smooth, and hence so is the surface SS.

Write HH for the class of a line in ℙℂ2\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}. Since B∈|4​H|B\in|4H|, the canonical bundle formula for a smooth double cover gives

KS=π∗​(Kℙℂ2+2​H)=π∗​(−H).K_{S}=\pi^{*}(K_{\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}}+2H)=\pi^{*}(-H).

Consequently −KS=π∗​H-K_{S}=\pi^{*}H is ample and

KS2=(π∗​H)2=2​H2=2.K_{S}^{2}=(\pi^{*}H)^{2}=2H^{2}=2.

Thus SS is a Del Pezzo surface of degree 22.

Define

G≔⟨ρ,σ,τ:ρ7=σ3=τ2=[τ,ρ]=[τ,σ]=1,σρσ−1=ρ4⟩≃(C7⋊C3)×C2,G\coloneqq\langle\rho,\sigma,\tau:\rho^{7}=\sigma^{3}=\tau^{2}=[\tau,\rho]=[\tau,\sigma]=1,\sigma\rho\sigma^{-1}=\rho^{4}\rangle\simeq(C_{7}\rtimes C_{3})\times C_{2},

and set

G7≔⟨ρ⟩,G3≔⟨σ⟩,G2≔⟨τ⟩,Gp≔{1}​(p∉{2,3,7}),G_{7}\coloneqq\langle{\rho}\rangle,\qquad G_{3}\coloneqq\langle{\sigma}\rangle,\qquad G_{2}\coloneqq\langle{\tau}\rangle,\qquad G_{p}\coloneqq\{1\}\,\,(p\notin\{2,3,7\}),

so that GpG_{p} is a cyclic Sylow pp-subgroup of GG for each prime pp.

Fix a primitive seventh root of unity ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C}. The formulas

ρ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\rho[x:y:z:w] =[ζx:ζ4y:ζ2z:w],\displaystyle=[\zeta x:\zeta^{4}y:\zeta^{2}z:w],
σ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\sigma[x:y:z:w] =[y:z:x:w],\displaystyle=[y:z:x:w],
τ[x:y:z:w]\displaystyle\tau[x:y:z:w] =[x:y:z:−w]\displaystyle=[x:y:z:-w]

define a faithful GG-action on SS.

Proposition 3.1.

The surface SS is GpG_{p}-very versal for every prime pp.

Proof.

If p∉{2,3,7}p\notin\{2,3,7\}, then GpG_{p} is trivial and the conclusion follows from the fact that SS is rational and Proposition 2.1(iii).

Suppose that p∈{2,7}p\in\{2,7\}. The inverse image of the tangent line y=0y=0 to BB at [1:0:0][1:0:0] is the cuspidal rational curve

C≔{y=0,w2=z3​x}⊂S.C\coloneqq\{y=0,\ w^{2}=z^{3}x\}\subset S.

Its normalization map is

ν:ℙℂ1⟶C⊂S,[u:v]⟼[u2:0:v2:uv3].\nu:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\longrightarrow C\subset S,\qquad[u:v]\longmapsto[u^{2}:0:v^{2}:uv^{3}].

Define actions of G2G_{2} and G7G_{7} on ℙℂ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}} by the formulas

τ[u:v]=[u:−v],ρ[u:v]=[u:ζ4v].\tau[u:v]=[u:-v],\qquad\rho[u:v]=[u:\zeta^{4}v].

The morphism ν\nu is equivariant for these actions:

ν(τ[u:v])=[u2:0:v2:−uv3]=τ(ν[u:v]),\nu(\tau[u:v])=[u^{2}:0:v^{2}:-uv^{3}]=\tau(\nu[u:v]),
ν(ρ[u:v])=[u2:0:ζv2:ζ5uv3]=[ζu2:0:ζ2v2:uv3]=ρ(ν[u:v]).\nu(\rho[u:v])=[u^{2}:0:\zeta v^{2}:\zeta^{5}uv^{3}]=[\zeta u^{2}:0:\zeta^{2}v^{2}:uv^{3}]=\rho(\nu[u:v]).

It follows from Lemma 2.2 that SS is G2G_{2}-very versal and G7G_{7}-very versal.

It remains to consider the case p=3p=3. Let

L≔{x+y+z=0}⊂ℙℂ2.L\coloneqq\{x+y+z=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}.

Substituting z=−x−yz=-x-y, we obtain f⁡(x,y,−x−y)=−(x2+x​y+y2)2f(x,y,-x-y)=-(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})^{2}. Thus the inverse image of LL in SS is the union of the two curves

E±={x+y+z=0,w=±i(x2+xy+y2)}.E_{\pm}=\{x+y+z=0,\quad w=\pm i(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})\}.

Each of these curves is isomorphic to ℙℂ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}. Indeed, the restriction of π\pi induces an isomorphism E±→LE_{\pm}\to L, whose inverse is

[x:y:z]⟼[x:y:z:±i(x2+xy+y2)].[x:y:z]\longmapsto[x:y:z:\pm i(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})].

Moreover, since σ⁡(L)=L\sigma(L)=L, the two irreducible components E+E_{+} and E−E_{-} of π−1​(L)\pi^{-1}(L) are permuted by σ\sigma. Since σ\sigma has order 33, its induced permutation of the two-element set {E+,E−}\{E_{+},E_{-}\} is trivial, that is, σ\sigma preserves each of E+E_{+} and E−E_{-}. Consequently, identifying E+E_{+} with ℙℂ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}, the inclusion E+↪SE_{+}\hookrightarrow S yields a nonconstant G3G_{3}-equivariant morphism ℙℂ1→S\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\to S. By Lemma 2.2, we conclude that SS is G3G_{3}-very versal. ∎

Proposition 3.2.

We have edℂ⁡(G)=3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)=3. In particular, the GG-variety SS is not versal.

Proof.

We first prove that edℂ⁡(G)>2\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)>2. Since GG is not trivial, cyclic, or dihedral of order 2​n2n with nn odd, we have edℂ⁡(G)>1\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)>1; see [Dun13, Proposition 2.4(c) and (d)]. Suppose that edℂ⁡(G)=2\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)=2. Since the center of GG is nontrivial, [Dun13, Proposition 2.5] implies that GG embeds into GL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). In particular, the subgroup

H≔⟨ρ,σ⟩≃C7⋊C3H\coloneqq\langle{\rho,\sigma}\rangle\simeq C_{7}\rtimes C_{3}

has a faithful two-dimensional complex representation VV.

Since ρ\rho has finite order, its action on VV is diagonalizable. Let v∈Vv\in V be a ρ\rho-eigenvector, and let λ∈μ7​(ℂ)\lambda\in\mu_{7}(\mathbb{C}) be its eigenvalue. From the relations ρ7=σ3=1\rho^{7}=\sigma^{3}=1 and σ​ρ​σ−1=ρ4\sigma\rho\sigma^{-1}=\rho^{4}, we obtain

ρ⁡(σ​v)=σ​ρ2​v=λ2​σ​v,ρ⁡(σ2​v)=σ2​ρ4​v=λ4​σ2​v.\rho(\sigma v)=\sigma\rho^{2}v=\lambda^{2}\sigma v,\qquad\rho(\sigma^{2}v)=\sigma^{2}\rho^{4}v=\lambda^{4}\sigma^{2}v.

Thus vv, σ​v\sigma v, and σ2​v\sigma^{2}v are ρ\rho-eigenvectors with eigenvalues λ\lambda, λ2\lambda^{2}, and λ4\lambda^{4}, respectively. If λ≠1\lambda\neq 1, these three eigenvalues are distinct, which is impossible because VV has dimension 22. Therefore every eigenvalue of ρ\rho is equal to 11. Since ρ\rho is diagonalizable, we deduce that it acts trivially on VV, contradicting the faithfulness of the representation. Hence edℂ⁡(G)>2\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)>2.

For the reverse inequality, the formulas

φ⁡(ρ)=(ζ000ζ4000ζ2),φ⁡(σ)=(010001100),φ⁡(τ)=(−1000−1000−1)\varphi(\rho)=\begin{pmatrix}\zeta&0&0\\ 0&\zeta^{4}&0\\ 0&0&\zeta^{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\varphi(\sigma)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 1&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\varphi(\tau)=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 0&-1&0\\ 0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}

define a faithful three-dimensional complex representation of GG. Thus edℂ⁡(G)≤3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)\leq 3. We conclude that edℂ⁡(G)=3\operatorname{ed}_{\mathbb{C}}(G)=3. The fact that SS is not GG-versal now follows from the definition of essential dimension. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

The conclusion follows from Proposition 3.1 and Proposition 3.2. ∎
